info.title: Farthing API
info.summary: Agentic checkout. Give it a product URL and a plain-English request; it drives a real browser to a completed purchase and asks a human only when it must.
info.description:
The HTTP API is the product. Everything an integration needs — creating checkouts, answering the questions a run stops on, storing buyers, issuing scoped keys — is here.

A checkout is asynchronous and pauses for humans. `POST /v1/checkouts` returns in milliseconds with a `queued` object; the run itself takes minutes and may park on a `pendingUserAction` for up to ten. Poll `GET /v1/checkouts/{id}` (unmetered) or register a webhook endpoint.

Not covered by this spec: the live-view embed (`GET /embed/{checkoutId}` and `GET /embed/{checkoutId}/stream`). Those are consumed by a browser, authenticate with a short-lived JWT minted at `POST /v1/checkouts/{id}/embed-token` rather than with an API key, and return HTML and `text/event-stream`.

tags.name: Signup
tags.description: Self-serve account creation. The only unauthenticated write on the API.

tags.name: Checkouts
tags.description: Create a run, poll it, cancel it, and answer what it asks.

tags.name: Buyer profiles
tags.description: Reusable identity and shipping details, referenced by id when creating a checkout.

tags.name: Buyer sessions
tags.description: Stored merchant logins captured by a `credentials` action. Read-only metadata and revocation.

tags.name: Webhooks
tags.description: Endpoints that receive `checkout.status_changed` with an HMAC-SHA256 signature.

tags.name: API keys
tags.description: Self-serve key issuance and revocation. Keys carry scopes; a key can never mint one broader than itself.

tags.name: Usage
tags.description: Completed checkouts by day, and gross merchandise volume by currency.

get.description: Unauthenticated. Returns immediately; does not touch the database.

post.description:
Creates a sandbox-only tenant and returns one `ck_test_` key, shown exactly once.

A sandbox tenant runs the entire product — real browser, real storefront, real card entry, a genuinely placed order — but only against merchants Farthing controls. It cannot reach a real merchant and cannot mint a `live` key until the account is activated.

Unauthenticated, and rate limited on its own terms: 3 signups per hour per source IP, 200 per 24 hours platform-wide.

requestBody.description: Optional. An empty body is valid.

name.description: Your account name. Defaults to `email`, then to `"sandbox tenant"`.

email.description: Contact address. Not verified, not emailed.

429.description: Signup rate limit hit — per-IP or platform-wide.

example.message: Too many signups from this address. Try again later.

post.description:
Returns immediately with a `queued` checkout. The run happens asynchronously in a durable orchestrator, so a client crash or a network blip never orphans a half-finished purchase.

Requires the `checkouts.write` scope.

**Retries.** Send an `Idempotency-Key` header and a duplicate `POST` returns the original checkout with `200` rather than buying the item twice. Without one, two identical requests are two runs and two orders. A key is live for 24 hours from the creation of the checkout that claimed it; after that the same string starts a new purchase.

**Strict body.** An unrecognised top-level field is a `400`. A misspelled `subjectt` used to return `201` with an untagged checkout the whole account could read, and an isolation control that fails open on a typo is not a control.

target.request: buy this in medium, cheapest delivery

200.description: An `Idempotency-Key` replay: this key has already been used with this body. The original checkout, **as it is now** — not a recording of the original `201`, so the status may have moved on and a `pendingUserAction` may already be waiting. Nothing was created, no quota was consumed, and no second browser was launched.

buy this in medium, cheapest delivery

Reusing a key for a different purchase is a caller bug — usually a key derived from the attempt rather than from the purchase — so it is refused rather than silently answered with a checkout for something else.

get.description:
Cursor-paginated summaries, newest first. Deliberately a summary rather than the full object: the full shape carries the whole event timeline, which is exactly what a list view must not fetch.

Requires the `checkouts.read` scope.

`?subject=` narrows the page to one end user, and each row carries `subject` when the checkout has one. A subject-bound key is already narrowed to its own end user; asking for another's is a `403`.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Filter to one status. An unrecognised value is a `400`, not an empty page.

parameters.name: subject
parameters.description:
Filter to one end user. Composes with `status`, `limit` and `cursor`; a subject with no checkouts is an empty page, not an error.

A subject-bound key does not need this — its page is already narrowed to one person. Passing its own subject is fine; naming a different one is a `403`, refused rather than quietly ignored.

Validated like every other subject: 1 to 200 characters, or `400`.

nextCursor.description: Pass back as `?cursor=`. `null` means this was the last page.

data.subject: user_a91f
data.request: buy this in medium, cheapest delivery

value.message: 'limit' must be an integer between 1 and 100
'cursor' must be an ISO 8601 timestamp from a previous nextCursor

403.description: A missing scope, a suspended tenant, or a subject-bound key asking for another end user's rows with `?subject=`.

value.message: This API key is missing the 'checkouts.read' scope.

otherSubject.summary: A bound key filtering for somebody else

value.message: This API key is bound to subject 'user_a91f' and cannot act for another.

get.description:
The whole current state in one object: status, the append-only `progressItems` timeline, the `pendingUserAction` if the run is blocked, and the `receipt` once it has succeeded.

This is the endpoint you poll. Reads are not rate limited; a 3–5 second interval is right for a process that takes minutes.

Requires the `checkouts.read` scope.

progressItems.label: This product comes in multiple options — pick one to continue.

pendingUserAction.message: This product comes in multiple options — pick one to continue.

data.message: Order total 61.40 USD exceeds maxCost 60.00 USD

delete.description:
Accepted, not applied. The cancellation is enqueued; the run stops, the browser is torn down, and the checkout lands on `cancelled` shortly after. Poll to observe it.

Cancelling an already-terminal checkout is a no-op that still returns `202`.

Requires the `checkouts.write` scope.

post.description:
Returns a short-lived JWT pinned to this one checkout, and the URL to open with it. The checkout id alone gets you nothing — the token is what gates the stream.

The view is read-only by construction: no input path exists from the embed to the browser.

Requires the `checkouts.write` scope (it is a `POST`).

200.description: Token minted. Expires 10 minutes from now.

parameters.name: actionId
parameters.description: The `pendingUserAction.id` from the checkout. A new action gets a new id every time — never cache one.

post.summary: Answer or decline a user action
post.description:
Submit the values described by the action's `responseSchema`, or decline to abandon the purchase. Declining is a first-class outcome, not an error path: the run stops immediately and the checkout fails with `user_cancelled`.

The response is the full checkout, re-serialized, with `pendingUserAction` gone.

Values for `card`, `credentials` and `otp` actions are fully redacted in the audit record and the raw copy goes to a transient, delete-on-read store consumed by the one step that types it.

Requires the `checkouts.write` scope.

404.description: No such checkout, or no such action on this checkout.

409.description: The action is no longer pending. This is also your idempotency signal — if your own retry gets `Action already submitted`, the first attempt landed.

post.description:
Every field is optional — `{}` is a valid profile — but the agent can only fill what you gave it. Values are stored and typed exactly as sent: no normalisation, no address validation, no correction.

One profile per end user. A profile is the identity that stored merchant sessions hang off, so reusing one across unrelated buyers would share their merchant logins.

Requires the `buyer-profiles.write` scope.

Set `subject` to say which of your end users this profile is for. A key bound to that subject can then reach it and no other end user's key can.

201.description: Created. Omitted sub-objects come back as `null`, not `{}`.

get.description:
Cursor-paginated, newest first.

Requires the `buyer-profiles.read` scope.

patch.description:
Partial at the top level, wholesale underneath. `name`, `contact` and `shipping` are each stored as one JSON document: omit a key and that document is untouched; supply one and it **replaces** the old document entirely.

That is deliberate. Merging half an address into an old one is how you ship a parcel to a street in the wrong city — so send a whole `shipping` object or none at all.

An empty body is a `400`, not a no-op. Send `"shipping": null` to clear a document outright — which is how an address you no longer want held is removed short of deleting the whole profile. `{}` stores an empty object instead, which is a different thing.

Requires the `buyer-profiles.write` scope.

relabel.summary: Change only the label; name/contact/shipping untouched

400.description: Type mismatch, or nothing to update.

delete.description:
A real delete, not a tombstone. This is the path for honouring "remove what you hold about me".

What goes and what stays is decided by the schema, not by a cleanup job:

- Checkouts that referenced this profile **survive** with their `buyerProfileId` set to null, so purchase history outlives the identity.
- Buyer sessions for this profile — the stored merchant logins — **cascade away**. That is the point of deleting, not a side effect.

Requires the `buyer-profiles.write` scope.

get.description:
Metadata only. The cookie blob itself is encrypted at rest and is never returned by any endpoint.

Sessions are created only by checkout runs — a `credentials` login, or a refresh on a later success — so there is no `POST` here.

When the session vault is disabled on the deployment, this returns an empty list with `vaultEnabled: false` rather than an error.

Requires the `buyer-sessions.read` scope.

vaultEnabled.description: `false` means the deployment has no session vault configured; `sessions` is then always empty.

delete.description:
A row delete. The next checkout at that merchant for that buyer starts logged out and will raise a `credentials` action again if the site demands one.

Requires the `buyer-sessions.write` scope.

404.description: No such session, or not yours.

post.description:
The signing secret is returned exactly once, here. Store it — nothing can recover it.

Requires the `webhooks.write` scope.

A subject-bound key cannot manage webhook endpoints. One endpoint receives the transitions of every checkout the tenant runs, for every end user, so registering or reading them from a single person's key would be a way to subscribe to everyone else's activity. `403`.

url.description: Must be `https://`. `http://localhost` and `http://127.0.0.1` are allowed for development.

secret.description: `whsec_…`. Shown once. Used to verify the `t=…,v1=…` signature header.

get.description:
Active endpoints only — revoked ones are excluded. Never returns a secret.

Answers `{ data, endpoints, nextCursor }`: read `data`, the field the checkout and buyer-profile lists also use. `endpoints` is the same array under its original name, and `nextCursor` is always `null` because this collection is not paged.

Requires the `webhooks.read` scope.

A subject-bound key cannot manage webhook endpoints. One endpoint receives the transitions of every checkout the tenant runs, for every end user, so registering or reading them from a single person's key would be a way to subscribe to everyone else's activity. `403`.

200.description: Active endpoints, newest first. Revoked ones are excluded. Not paged.

data.description: The collection. Read this one — it is the field the checkout and buyer-profile lists answer with too. (`GET /v1/buyer-sessions` is the one list route that has not converged: it answers `{ sessions, vaultEnabled }`.)

endpoints.description: The same array under the field's original name, kept because existing callers read it. Identical contents; prefer `data` in new code.

nextCursor.description: Always `null` here — the collection is small and tenant-bounded, so there is nothing to page. Present so a generic list client needs no special case.

delete.description:
Revocation is a timestamp, not a row delete. Deliveries stop immediately and the endpoint drops out of the list.

Requires the `webhooks.write` scope.

A subject-bound key cannot manage webhook endpoints. `403`.

404.description: Unknown, another tenant's, or already revoked.

post.description:
The plaintext key is returned exactly once, here. Only `sha256(key)` is stored — no endpoint, support process or database query can recover it.

**Scopes.** Omit `scopes` and the key gets `["*"]`, full access, which is what a key has always meant here. Supply an array to narrow it. A key can never mint a key with scopes it does not itself hold, so `api-keys.write` is not a back door to `*`.

**Mode.** Two independent `403`s guard a `live` key: a sandbox-only account cannot create one, and a `ck_test_` key cannot issue one however activated the account is. Authority passes down, never sideways — otherwise the sandbox confinement a test key exists to provide would be one `POST` deep. Mode is fixed at creation; there is no promotion path. A consequence worth planning for: a self-serve signup only ever holds `ck_test_` keys, so the first `ck_live_` key on a newly activated account cannot be minted through this endpoint and has to be issued during activation.

An empty body is valid and produces a full-access `test` key.

Requires the `api-keys.write` scope.

mode.description: `test` keys are confined to sandbox merchants no matter how the account is configured.

subject.description:
Bind the key to one of your end users — your own opaque id, 1 to 200 characters after trimming. **Omit for a tenant-wide key**, which is what every key issued before this existed already is. `""` is a `400`, not a tenant-wide key by another name.

A bound key sees and creates only that subject's checkouts and buyer profiles, and is refused outright on the account-wide endpoints (`GET`/`DELETE /v1/api-keys`, `/v1/usage`, `/v1/webhooks`).

Minting from a bound key **inherits** the binding: omitting `subject` gives another key for the same end user, not a tenant-wide one, and naming a different subject is a `403`. Fixed at creation — there is no rebinding and no unbinding.

schema.description: The top level is strict: an unrecognised field is a `400` with an `unrecognized_keys` issue, not a field the server drops for you. The field most worth misspelling here is `subject`, and a `201` carrying an untagged row is an isolation control that failed open on a typo.

narrow.summary: An agent that may only run checkouts

boundToOneEndUser.summary: A key that can only ever act for one end user

201.description: Created. `key` appears here and nowhere else, ever.

400.description: Bad `mode`, or a scope string that is not in the valid set.

403.description: A sandbox-only account asking for a live key, a test key asking for a live key, or an attempt to escalate scopes or subject. Authority passes down, never sideways.

value.message: This account is sandbox-only. Live keys require activation.

escalation.summary: A narrow key trying to mint a broader one

value.message: A key cannot grant scopes it does not itself hold.

modeEscalation.summary: A test key trying to mint a live key

value.message: A test key cannot issue a live key. Use a live key, or activate the account.

subjectEscalation.summary: A subject-bound key trying to issue a key for someone else

value.message: This API key is bound to subject 'user_a91f' and cannot issue keys for another.

get.description:
Answers `{ data, keys, nextCursor }`: `data` is the field the checkout and buyer-profile lists also use and the one to read, `keys` is the same array under its original name, and `nextCursor` is always `null` because this collection is not paged. Newest first. **Revoked keys are included**, with `revokedAt` set — filter client-side if you only want active ones.

Listing never returns a secret. `keyPrefix` is the most a list can show.

Requires the `api-keys.read` scope.

A subject-bound key cannot call this: the key list is a tenant-wide fact, and a credential acting for one end user must not be able to enumerate its siblings. `403`.

200.description: Every key on the tenant, newest first, revoked ones included. Not paged.

data.description: The collection. Read this one — it is the field the checkout and buyer-profile lists answer with too. (`GET /v1/buyer-sessions` is the one list route that has not converged: it answers `{ sessions, vaultEnabled }`.)

keys.description: The same array under the field's original name, kept because existing callers read it. Identical contents; prefer `data` in new code.

nextCursor.description: Always `null` here — the collection is small and tenant-bounded, so there is nothing to page. Present so a generic list client needs no special case.

delete.description:
Takes effect immediately. Revocation is a timestamp, not a row delete — knowing which key was live when matters more than a tidy table if one is ever abused.

Nothing stops a key revoking itself. Revoke the old key only after the new one's traffic has taken over.

Requires the `api-keys.write` scope.

A subject-bound key cannot call this. Revocation is a tenant-wide power — left open, one end user's key could take the account's own key offline. `403`.

404.description: Covers all three cases: unknown id, another tenant's key, already revoked.

example.message: Key not found or already revoked

get.description:
Completed checkouts only. Attempts are never metered — charging for attempts would mean earning more when the agent fails, which is backwards for a product whose entire problem is reliability.

The default window is the current calendar month (UTC), which is the unit tenants are billed in.

Requires the `usage.read` scope.

A subject-bound key cannot call this. Billing is between us and the tenant; an end user's key reading the account's total spend and order volume would be a leak between your own customers. `403`.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Inclusive start. Any `Date`-parseable string. Defaults to the first instant of the current UTC month.

bearerAuth.description: `Authorization: Bearer ck_test_…` or `ck_live_…`. There is no other auth scheme — no query-string keys, no request signing, no OAuth.

CheckoutId.name: id
CheckoutId.description: The checkout id returned at creation.

Limit.name: limit
Limit.description: Page size. Must be an integer from 1 to 100; anything else is a `400`.

Cursor.name: cursor
Cursor.description: The previous page's `nextCursor` — an ISO 8601 timestamp. Returns rows created strictly before it.

IdempotencyKey.name: Idempotency-Key
IdempotencyKey.description:
Makes a create safe to retry. A second request with the same key returns the **original** checkout with `200` instead of starting a second run; the same key with a different body is a `409`.

Strongly recommended on every create. A `POST` that times out after the server accepted it is indistinguishable, from the caller's side, from one that never landed, and every autonomous caller retries a timeout by default — so without this header the worst failure mode of the product is reachable by an ordinary network blip.

The request body is hashed with its object keys sorted and its defaults applied, so key order does not matter and `"constraints": {}` matches an omitted `constraints`. Keys are namespaced per (tenant, `subject`) and live 24 hours, measured from the creation of the checkout that claimed one. Inside the window a retry replays; outside it the key is released and the same string starts a new purchase. Release is an hourly background sweep, so the boundary is approximate to within an hour, and it clears the key off the checkout without otherwise touching the row. An empty or whitespace-only value is treated as absent.

Read by `POST /v1/checkouts` only; every other endpoint ignores it.

Unauthorized.description: Missing, malformed, invalid or revoked bearer token. There is no distinction between "never existed" and "revoked" — that difference is only useful to someone probing.

Forbidden.description: The key is missing the scope this route requires, the tenant is suspended, or the key is bound to one end user and this route answers an account-wide question.

value.message: This API key is missing the 'buyer-profiles.read' scope.

subjectBound.summary: A subject-bound key reaching for a tenant-wide fact

value.message: A subject-bound key cannot read account usage.

ValidationError.description: The body did not parse. `issues` carries the raw Zod issues, which are precise enough to point at the offending field.

CheckoutNotFound.description: No such checkout, or it belongs to another tenant — the two are not distinguished.

ProfileNotFound.description: No such profile, or it belongs to another tenant.

Error.title: Error
Error.description: Every error is this object. There are no error codes: match on the HTTP status, treat `message` as text for a human.

issues.description: Raw Zod issues. `path` is the machine-readable part. Additional fields appear depending on `code` (`validation`, `expected`, `received`, …) — do not treat the list below as exhaustive.

ScopeError.title: ScopeError
ScopeError.description: An out-of-scope request. `requiredScope` saves you parsing the message.

EscalationError.title: EscalationError
EscalationError.description: Returned when a key tries to mint a key with scopes it does not hold.

heldScopes.description: What the authenticating key actually holds.

validScopes.description: The complete valid set, so you never have to guess.

SandboxError.title: SandboxError
SandboxError.description: Sandbox confinement. Raised when the account is sandbox-only, or when the request arrived on a `ck_test_` key — the two triggers are independent.

IdempotencyConflict.title: IdempotencyConflict
IdempotencyConflict.description: `POST /v1/checkouts` only. `checkoutId` names the checkout the key already refers to, so you can inspect it and decide whether the retry was the mistake or the key was.

Scope.title: Scope
Scope.description: `<resource>.read` or `<resource>.write`, or the wildcard `*`. `write` implies `read` on the same resource. Resources are exactly the route groups under `/v1`.

CheckoutStatus.title: CheckoutStatus
CheckoutStatus.description: `succeeded`, `failed` and `cancelled` are terminal; nothing leaves them.

FailureReason.title: FailureReason
FailureReason.description: A closed set of four. The human-readable detail lives in the final `terminal` progress item's `data.message`, not here.

kind.description: Only one kind exists. There is no product search — you bring the URL.

url.description: The product or cart page to start from.

request.description: Plain English, for the agent. `"buy this in medium, cheapest delivery"`. A request that unambiguously names an option value skips the variant question entirely.

merchantContext.description: Anything the agent should know about this merchant that the page will not tell it.

allowedDomains.description:
Extra hostnames the run may navigate to beyond the target's own domain — e.g. a marketplace's separate auth domain. Hostnames only: no scheme, no path.

This set is fixed before the run starts and cannot grow at runtime, which is what stops untrusted page text steering a session holding buyer PII somewhere else.

countryCode.description: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 for the merchant. Selects the residential proxy exit so the merchant sees a local visitor. Inferred from the URL's ccTLD when omitted.

maxCost.description:
Spending ceiling for this checkout, checked before a card is ever requested. Omitting it means no cost enforcement at all.

A strong guardrail, not a hard ceiling: the order-total check depends on reading a total off the merchant's page, and if none can be parsed there is nothing to compare. The real ceiling should be the card.

ProgressItem.title: ProgressItem
ProgressItem.description: One entry on the append-only timeline.

kind.description: `intent_started`, `step`, `user_action`, `terminal`, and others as the engines grow. Treat unknown kinds as informational.

label.description: Written for a person. Render as-is.

data.description: Structured detail for this entry. `user_action` items carry `key`; the final `terminal` item on a failure carries `reason` and `message`.

sequence.description: Per-checkout, monotonic from 1. Track the highest you have seen to stream only what is new.

PendingUserAction.title: PendingUserAction
PendingUserAction.description: Present only while the run is blocked. At most one per checkout at a time.

id.description: Goes in the submit URL. A new action gets a new id every time — never cache one.

key.description:
What is being asked for. Branch on this, not on the shape of `responseSchema`.

The known set: `variant` (which size/colour — answerable by an agent), `shipping` (a delivery address — answerable if your app holds one), `card`, `credentials`, `otp` (all three come from the human, never from an agent's context). Tier 2 can raise a short slug of its own for something unanticipated; treat unknown keys as "route this to a person".

Absent on actions raised before this field existed.

message.description: Written for a person, in the context of this specific page. Render it as-is.

responseSchema.description: A real JSON Schema for the object you must send back as `values`. Always `{"type":"object","additionalProperties":false,…}` with a `required` array and a `properties` map; every property is `type: "string"`.

expiresAt.description: Authoritative. Default TTL is 10 minutes. Past this instant, answering fails and the checkout fails with `user_action_expired`.

detectedTotal.description: The merchant's own order total, shipping and tax included, read off the live page when the run stopped to ask. Present on card actions; best-effort, and currency may be absent. Show it to the user before answering — receipt.total only exists after the money has moved.

merchantOrderId.description: The merchant's own format. Do not parse it.

evidence.description: What the agent saw at confirmation — typically `{ "url": "…/thank_you" }`.

Checkout.title: Checkout
Checkout.description: The whole state of one run. This is what you poll.

subject.description: Your own id for the end user this purchase is for. **Absent** when the checkout is not tagged to one. Set explicitly at creation, or stamped from the authenticating key's binding.

buyerProfileId.description: Absent when no profile was attached, and absent after the referenced profile was deleted.

metadata.description: Yours. Stored and echoed back untouched; never sent to a merchant, and not searchable.

browser.description: Present once a browser session exists. Not a URL you can watch at — a pointer to the endpoint that mints one.

embedTokenUrl.description: `POST` here to mint a live-view token.

progressItems.description: Append-only, ordered by `sequence`. Build your UI around this rather than a spinner.

CheckoutSummary.title: CheckoutSummary
CheckoutSummary.description: The list-endpoint shape. No timeline — fetch the full object when you need one.

subject.description: Your own id for the end user this checkout is for. **Absent** when the checkout is not tagged to one — the same convention as the full object.

receipt.description: Present once a receipt exists. Total and order id only — no `evidence` on the summary.

pendingUserActionId.description: Present when this checkout is blocked. Fetch the checkout to see what it is asking for.

CheckoutCreate.title: CheckoutCreate

buyerProfileId.description:
Must belong to your tenant, or the request is a `400`. Without one the agent has no address, and on most merchants that is where the run stops — or it raises a `shipping` action.

Checked against **this checkout's** `subject`, not the authenticating key's. A subject-bound key naming another end user's profile gets the same `400 buyerProfileId not found` — from where it stands the profile does not exist. A tenant-wide key naming one end user's profile alongside another's `subject` gets a `403` naming both. An untagged profile on a tagged checkout is allowed, and so is the reverse, so subjects can be adopted incrementally.

subject.description:
Your own opaque id for one of your end users. 1 to 200 characters after trimming; never parsed, never validated against anything, and never sent to a merchant. An empty or whitespace-only value is a `400` — a subject that means nothing reads as isolation you do not have.

On a key bound to a subject this is filled in for you: omit it and the row is stamped with the key's subject, name a different one and the request is a `403`. On a tenant-wide key it is how a row gets tagged in the first place.

It also namespaces the `Idempotency-Key`: two end users may pick the same key string without colliding. `GET /v1/checkouts?subject=` filters the list by it, and `checkout.status_changed` deliveries carry it.

metadata.description: Anything you want echoed back on every poll.

CheckoutCreate.description:
The top level is strict: an unrecognised field is a `400` with an `unrecognized_keys` issue, not a field the server drops for you. The field most worth misspelling here is `subject`, and a `201` carrying an untagged row is an isolation control that failed open on a typo.

`target`, `constraints` and `metadata` stay permissive inside — they are extension points, and unknown keys within them are ignored.

values.description: Exactly the keys named in the action's `responseSchema.properties`. Send strings — the engines read them as strings. Required even if empty.

reason.description: Free text, stored on the action for your own audit.

BuyerName.description: Also used as the cardholder name at the payment step, which is why the card action never asks for one.
BuyerName.title: BuyerName

email.description: Where the merchant's order confirmation goes. Most checkouts refuse to proceed without it.

phone.description: Required by a fair number of merchants, particularly delivery.

addressLines.description: Only the **first** line is filled on the Shopify tier. Put an apartment number on line one if it matters.

administrativeAreaCode.description: State / province. Send the short code (`KY`, `ON`). Effectively required for US and CA addresses — Shopify offers no shipping method without it, and with no shipping method the order can never be placed.

countryCode.description: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2. Filled before the state, since changing country repopulates the province list.

BuyerProfileCreate.title: BuyerProfileCreate
BuyerProfileCreate.description:
Every field is optional — `{}` is a valid profile — but the agent can only fill what you gave it.

The top level is strict: an unrecognised field is a `400` with an `unrecognized_keys` issue, not a field the server drops for you. The field most worth misspelling here is `subject`, and a `201` carrying an untagged row is an isolation control that failed open on a typo. The nested `name`, `contact` and `shipping` objects are not strict. `PATCH` is strict in the same way.

label.description: Yours, for bookkeeping. Never sent to a merchant.

subject.description:
Your own opaque id for one of your end users. 1 to 200 characters after trimming; never parsed, never validated against anything, and never sent to a merchant. An empty or whitespace-only value is a `400` — a subject that means nothing reads as isolation you do not have.

On a key bound to a subject this is filled in for you: omit it and the row is stamped with the key's subject, name a different one and the request is a `403`. On a tenant-wide key it is how a row gets tagged in the first place.

**Create-only.** A profile cannot be reassigned to another end user afterwards: `PATCH` with `subject` is a `400`.

BuyerProfilePatch.title: BuyerProfilePatch
BuyerProfilePatch.description:
Partial at the top level only: omit a key and that document is untouched, supply one and it is **replaced wholesale**. There is no deep merge. `null` clears a document outright.

Strict: any key outside these four — `subject` in particular — is a `400` rather than a silently dropped field, because a caller trying to move a profile to another end user should be told it did not happen.

label.description: Yours, for bookkeeping. Never sent to a merchant. `null` clears it.

subject.description: Your own id for the end user this profile belongs to, or `null` when it is not tagged to one. Always present — unlike a checkout, which omits the field entirely. Fixed at creation.

BuyerSession.title: BuyerSession
BuyerSession.description: Metadata about a stored merchant login. The cookies themselves are encrypted at rest and never returned.

lastDeliveryStatus.description: The HTTP status your endpoint last answered with.

scopes.description: `["*"]` for a full-access key, including every key issued before scopes existed.

subject.description: The end user this key acts for, or `null` for a tenant-wide key. Always present here, unlike on the creation response. This listing is the only place to audit which of your keys act for whom — and a subject-bound key cannot read it.

keyPrefix.description: The first 16 characters. Safe to store and display — it identifies which key without being one.

lastUsedAt.description: Written best-effort on every authenticated request; never blocks it. A good rotation signal, not an audit log.

subject.description: The end user this key acts for. **Present only when the key is bound** — a tenant-wide key's creation response has no `subject` field at all.

key.description: The plaintext key. Returned here and nowhere else, ever.

sandboxMerchants.description: The only hosts this account can check out at until it is activated.

apiKey.description: Shown once. Only a SHA-256 hash is stored — nothing can recover it.

token.description: A JWT pinned to this one checkout.

url.description: The viewer page, token already in the query string. Put it in an iframe.

expiresAt.description: 10 minutes from minting. Mint another when it lapses.

byDay.description: Completed checkouts per **UTC day**, cut at UTC midnight to match `from`, `to` and every other timestamp the API returns — the bucket a checkout lands in never depends on the server's timezone or yours. Days with no completions are omitted, not zero-filled.

merchandiseVolume.description: Gross merchandise volume by currency. Reporting only — billing is per completed checkout, not a percentage.

WebhookEvent.title: WebhookEvent
WebhookEvent.description: The body of a `checkout.status_changed` delivery. It says **that** something changed, not what the checkout now looks like: fetch `GET /v1/checkouts/{checkoutId}` for the state.

type.description: The only event type today. Switch on it anyway and ignore what you do not recognise.

subject.description:
Your own id for the end user this checkout is for. **Absent** when the checkout is not tagged to one.

An endpoint is tenant-wide — it receives every end user's transitions — so this is what lets a delivery be routed to the right person without a callback or a map of your own.

createdAt.description: When the transition was dispatched, stamped once — a retried delivery carries the original event time.

post.description: Delivered to every active endpoint on the tenant when a checkout moves status. `queued` does not fire — creation is synchronous and the caller already holds the object. Delivery is best-effort with a 10-second timeout and 3 retries, carries no event id and no ordering guarantee, so treat it as a doorbell and make the handler idempotent against the state you fetch.

parameters.name: x-checkoutvia-signature
parameters.description: `t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex>`. `v1` is `HMAC-SHA256(secret, "<t>.<raw body>")` with the endpoint's `whsec_…` secret. Verify against the raw request bytes, before any JSON parse.

untagged.summary: An untagged checkout — no subject field at all

2XX.description: Acknowledged. Return quickly and do the work out of band — anything slower than 10 seconds is treated as a failure and retried.

4XX.description: Anything outside `2xx` counts as a failure and is retried. `410 Gone` does not auto-disable the endpoint — revoke it with `DELETE /v1/webhooks/{id}`.
